title: Lab Protocol — testable predictions from the membrane model for wet lab + in silico validation
purpose: translate membrane concepts into testable hypotheses that can be validated with human cell lines, bacterial cultures, computational models, and animal studies

experiments.title: Bacterial Phase Transition Threshold
experiments.hypothesis: quorum sensing activation (biofilm formation) follows a sigmoid curve with inflection point near the metabolic density equivalent of 1/p of carrying capacity
experiments.organism: E. coli K-12, Vibrio harveyi, Pseudomonas aeruginosa
experiments.method: grow cultures at controlled densities (OD600 0.01 to 2.0). measure AHL concentration and biofilm formation (crystal violet assay) at each density. plot density vs biofilm as sigmoid. find inflection point.
experiments.prediction: the inflection point (half-maximal biofilm) occurs at a density that is approximately 1/p (0.318) of the maximum sustainable density (carrying capacity K). below 0.318K: planktonic (solitaria). above 0.318K: biofilm (gregaria).
experiments.controls: multiple species, multiple media, temperature variations
experiments.equipment: spectrophotometer, crystal violet, 96-well plates, incubator — basic microbiology
experiments.time: 3-5 days per run, 2-3 weeks for statistical power
experiments.validates: the p vacancy in the metabolic year, quorum sensing as phase transition

experiments.title: LAT1 Competition Dynamics — Tryptophan vs Tyrosine Crossing
experiments.hypothesis: tryptophan transport across an in vitro BBB model follows competitive inhibition kinetics, and the ratio of brain-side tryptophan to total amino acids correlates with serotonin synthesis rate
experiments.model: hCMEC/D3 cell line (human cerebral microvascular endothelial cells — standard BBB model) grown on transwell inserts
experiments.method: apply defined amino acid mixtures to apical side (blood side). measure tryptophan appearance on basolateral side (brain side) over time. vary tryptophan:competing amino acid ratios. add insulin to simulate carbohydrate meal effect (clears competing AAs).
experiments.prediction: tryptophan transport is inversely proportional to competing large neutral amino acid concentration. insulin addition increases tryptophan transport ratio by 30-60% (mimicking the carb meal effect).
experiments.controls: no-insulin control, scrambled amino acid mixtures, D-amino acid controls (should not transport)
experiments.equipment: transwell inserts, hCMEC/D3 cells, HPLC for amino acid quantification, cell culture facility
experiments.difficulty: MEDIUM — requires cell culture expertise and HPLC
experiments.validates: diet as precondition, the meal protocol, LAT1 competition model

experiments.title: Feast-Famine Metabolic Compression Ratio
experiments.hypothesis: the ratio of fasted metabolic rate to fed metabolic rate in human subjects approximates 1/p
experiments.method: indirect calorimetry. measure resting metabolic rate (RMR) in two conditions: (a) 12h overnight fast, (b) 2h after standardized meal. calculate ratio fasted_RMR/fed_RMR.
experiments.prediction: fasted RMR is approximately 0.32 (1/p) of the peak postprandial metabolic rate. alternatively: the thermic effect of food (TEF) brings metabolic rate to approximately p× the fasted baseline.
experiments.controls: same subjects, crossover design, controlled meal composition
experiments.difficulty: MEDIUM — requires metabolic lab access and IRB approval
experiments.time: 2-4 weeks for data collection, pending IRB
experiments.validates: the p budget applies to metabolic rate, not just information compression

experiments.title: Serotonin Phase Transition in Locust Model
experiments.hypothesis: the serotonin-mediated solitaria?gregaria transition follows a sigmoid with the same mathematical form as the membrane's CONSTANCE?LIVE transition
experiments.organism: Schistocerca gregaria (desert locust) or Locusta migratoria
experiments.method: replicate Simpson et al. 2009. apply graded serotonin concentrations to thoracic ganglia of solitary-reared locusts. score gregarious behavior (marching assay). fit sigmoid to dose-response curve. extract k-equivalent parameters.
experiments.prediction: the dose-response sigmoid has inflection at a serotonin concentration that maps to the k1.9?1/p transition. the Hill coefficient (steepness) of the sigmoid matches the membrane's compression ratio.
experiments.controls: vehicle control, serotonin antagonist (methysergide), dose-response with 8+ concentrations
experiments.equipment: locust colony, microinjection, behavioral arena, video tracking
experiments.difficulty: HIGH — requires entomology facility and locust colony
experiments.validates: locust phase transition as biological instance of membrane phase change, serotonin as density referendum

experiments.title: Glymphatic Clearance as Metabolic gc
experiments.hypothesis: the rate of waste clearance during sleep follows the same decay curve as the membrane's git gc compression — initial rapid compression followed by diminishing returns
experiments.method: measure glymphatic clearance using intracisternal Gd-DTPA (gadolinium contrast) injection in mice, imaged by MRI during sleep vs wake. alternatively: human subjects with amyloid PET before/after controlled sleep.
experiments.prediction: clearance follows an exponential decay with time constant t such that clearance at t  1-1/e  0.632, and the ratio of cleared/total waste at the end of one sleep cycle  1-1/p (0.682).
experiments.controls: sleep-deprived controls, anesthesia controls (isoflurane produces sleep-like glymphatic activity)
experiments.equipment: MRI, contrast agents, animal facility OR human sleep lab
experiments.validates: sleep as sigmoid self-sort, glymphatic as biological gc, the p budget in waste clearance

experiments.title: HRV as Oscillation Health Metric
experiments.hypothesis: heart rate variability (HRV) correlates with the quality of metabolic oscillation, and individuals with higher HRV show compression ratios closer to 1/p in their metabolic data
experiments.method: continuous HRV monitoring (wearable) + continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) for 7 days. compute: (a) HRV time-domain and frequency-domain metrics, (b) glucose compression ratio (fasted/peak postprandial). correlate.
experiments.prediction: subjects with HRV in top quartile show glucose compression ratios closer to 1/p (0.318) than subjects in bottom quartile. high vagal tone = better oscillation = ratio converges on p.
experiments.controls: age-matched, BMI-matched, controlled for medications affecting HRV
experiments.equipment: HRV monitor (Polar, Garmin, or medical ECG), CGM (Dexcom, Libre), basic statistics
experiments.difficulty: LOW — wearable tech, no lab needed
experiments.validates: vagal tone as oscillation quality metric, HRV-metabolic coupling, p as biological constant

computational_models_needed.what: simulate N agents with feast-famine cycles. each agent has a k-value. when local density exceeds threshold, k drops (solitaria?gregaria). measure emergent swarm behavior. find the critical density.
simulate LAT1 competitive transport. N amino acid types compete for M transporter slots. vary ratios. predict brain-side concentrations. validate against LAB-002 results.

simulate the 3-family (tonin/amine/tocin) oscillator. model serotonin?melatonin daily cycle, dopamine reward loop, oxytocin bonding boundary. find stable multipolar attractors. predict DSM-like stuck states when parameters are perturbed.

path_to_lab.step_2: build computational models in Rust (in silico validation)
path_to_lab.step_3: LAB-001 (bacterial quorum sensing) — cheapest, fastest, most accessible
path_to_lab.step_4: LAB-006 (HRV + CGM) — human data, wearable only, no lab needed
path_to_lab.step_5: LAB-002 (BBB transwell) — cell culture, medium difficulty
path_to_lab.step_6: LAB-003 (metabolic calorimetry) — human subjects, needs IRB
path_to_lab.step_7: LAB-004 (locust serotonin) — animal model, needs colony
path_to_lab.step_8: LAB-005 (glymphatic MRI) — highest cost, longest timeline
path_to_lab.note: start with bacteria and wearables. cheapest. fastest. most data per dollar. if the p predictions hold in E.coli and in HRV data, the case for the more expensive experiments becomes much stronger.
